extracted.intended_audience: general readers and historians interested in history of science, mathematical criticism, and 19th-century popular science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging self-styled mathematical reformers, popularizers, and 'paradoxers' — focusing on the legitimacy of analogies, logical/mathematical demonstration, clarity of notation, appropriateness of application, and openness to fair examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate properties with distinct entities in analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies used to illustrate doctrines should not treat properties as if they were distinct substances or persons (example: the sun, its light, and its heat being treated as three 'heavenly bodies' rather than one object with properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's critique: 'To adumbrate... the sun must be heavenly body, the light heavenly body, the heat heavenly body; and yet, not three heavenly bodies, but one heavenly body.' Avoid analogies that mistake attributes (properties) for ontological items; ensure mapping in analogies is correct and does not introduce category mistakes. The Dr. Sadler quote reinforces: 'The sun is one object with two properties, and these properties have a parallel not in the second and third persons of the Trinity, but in the attributes of Deity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical assertions must be demonstrable and consistent with established results
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold mathematical claims must be supported by correct demonstrations; unchecked or incorrect manipulations lead to absurd conclusions (example: Phillips' claimed series identity leading to the false equivalent 'the circumference of any circle is double of the diagonal of the cube on its diameter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mathematician 'instantly sees' the false equivalence: use internal consistency checks and known theorems to test new claims. A purported equality or transformation should be checked for convergence, correctness of manipulations (summation, limits), and compatibility with established geometry/analysis before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not teach or assert about subjects you do not understand
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal virtues (honesty, zeal, ability, courage) are insufficient when applied to teaching or advocating in disciplines about which one lacks knowledge: 'He applied them all to teaching matters about which he knew nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid enthusiastic advocacy or instruction outside one's competence. Verify domain knowledge before publishing instructional material or attempting reform; peer feedback and modesty about limits are advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical notation and terms must be defined and interpretable
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying mathematics (even to other fields), all symbols and terms must be explained; unexplained quantities render the work uninterpretable (Herbart's formula includes a 'jactura, v' which the author does not understand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide definitions and interpretive guidance for every introduced symbol and term. If the expression contains constants or technical words (e.g., 'jactura'), define them or show how they are measured; otherwise readers cannot evaluate the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grand universal denials of established mathematics without rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'all mathematics and physics are wrong' or that 'there is no differential calculus, no Taylor's theorem' are unacceptable without extraordinary proof (Walsh's stance exemplified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence: do not reject large, well-established bodies of theory on the basis of isolated arguments or rhetoric. Demonstrate specific errors carefully and address existing counter-evidence rather than issuing blanket denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary or sweeping solutions must be substantiated and open to refutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals of sweeping mathematical reforms or solutions (e.g., Wronski's asserted general solution of higher-degree equations using hundreds of auxiliary equations) must provide clear derivations and be prepared for formal refutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing general solutions or foundational reforms, present full proofs, worked examples, and anticipatory responses to likely objections. Submit claims to knowledgeable forums (academies, journals) and expect formal refutation; grandiosity without evidence undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite fair, public, and arithmetic examination of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments and aphorisms intended to overturn established views should be subject to 'a free and fair examination' and tested against arithmetic and demonstrative proof (Phillips' stated desire for examination of his aphorisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make work accessible for critical review, supply calculational checks, and outline which parts are empirical/arithmetic verifications versus philosophical assertions. Encourage transparent peer scrutiny rather than reliance on rhetoric about persecution or conspiracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer demonstration (evidence) over mere rejection of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom from dogmatic authority should not lead to 'contempt of demonstration'; the author insists that worship of reason implies prioritizing demonstrative proof over merely rejecting established authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims by the strength of argument and demonstration rather than by their novelty or opposition to authority. Rejection of authority must be accompanied by constructive, demonstrable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use satire appropriately but do not substitute it for evidence in serious claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire is a legitimate rhetorical tool to expose implausible a priori reasoning (Whately's parody on believing unlikely narratives), but when a claim is serious it requires evidence rather than mere banter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is to persuade on factual or historical questions, supply evidence and argument; satire can highlight logical absurdities but cannot replace proof when the claim is intended as literal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply mathematical methods to other disciplines only when they meaningfully support the thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications of mathematics outside pure mathematics (e.g., Herbart's attempt to apply mathematics to psychology) must actually furnish support for the thesis and be interpretable; mere formalism without substantive grounding is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure models relate to measurable aspects of the target domain, that parameters have clear interpretations, and that the mathematical conclusions have testable implications. If the model leaves key terms undefined or produces unintelligible auxiliary quantities, it fails as an applied argument.
